transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump announced the construction of a steel mill in Iowa today that he says
his tariffs made possible.
Iowa has closely watched House and Senate races with control of Congress at stake this
year.
And Pierre's Deepa Shivaram reports the plan is expected to create about 2,000 jobs but
isn't expected to begin producing steel until 2030.
Trump's announcement comes as Americans are souring on how they view Trump's handling
of the economy, and with the midterm elections just a little over a month away, the president
is running out of time to shift voters' perspectives.
"Today we're thrilled to announce that Massabi Metallics will be building the largest steel
plant in American history in the great state of Iowa.
It's the largest plant, one of the largest plants in the world."
The steel plant is being built by Massabi Metallics, a company based in Minnesota, though
the plant will be constructed in Iowa.
It's expected to produce 10 million tons of steel a year once it's fully built.
The $15 billion investment marks the first mega-steel plant to be built in the U.S. since
the 1960s, according to the White House.
Deepa Shivaram, NPR News, The White House.
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will not participate in an important climate change
case set for argument next week.
NPR's Kerry Johnson reports a court clerk did not provide an explanation in a letter
to the lawyers.
Environmental organizations and watchdog groups had been pressing Justice Alito to recuse
himself from the case, in which Boulder, Colorado, suing the energy companies Suncor and Exxon
over local harms due to climate change.
Alito does not own stock in those energy giants, but his financial disclosure says he has investments
in Phillips 66 and ConocoPhillips.
Consumer Watchdog says the decision to step aside is the right move.
Individual judges are required to step aside in cases where their impartiality might reasonably
be questioned, but at the Supreme Court, that decision is up to individual justices.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
SpaceX's Starship rocket reached orbit today for the first time, a key milestone in the
spacecraft's development, but as Central Florida Public Media's Brendan Byrne reports,
the mission was cut short.
Starship and its 33-engine booster launched from SpaceX's Starbase in Texas on a planned
10-hour mission.
The launch, for the most part, went as designed.
An engine on Starship did shut down about 30 seconds early, but Mission Control decided
it was still safe to continue its orbital path.
Just about three hours after liftoff, it splashed down the Pacific Ocean, near Hawaii.
It's unclear what caused the mission to end early.
During its time in orbit, Starship deployed more than two dozen Starlink satellites, a
new version that will help build SpaceX's global internet constellation in orbit.
SpaceX is counting on Starship to grow its commercial business, and NASA has tapped the
spacecraft to bring its astronauts to the lunar surface for future Artemis missions.
For NPR News, I'm Brendan Byrne in Orlando.
U.S. stocks pulled further from their record highs today.
This is NPR News.
The Trump administration is revoking the visas of 27 Latin American officials and their families,
including Bolivia's attorney general over accusations of corruption.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently visited conservative-leaning leaders in Colombia,
Ecuador, and Peru and pledged support for their efforts to combat drug and human trafficking.
Those leaders have said that the targeted officials were hindering their efforts to
fight crime.
The Cleveland Orchestra's strike is over after months of bargaining.
Kabir Bhatia from member station WKSU has more.
Bodana Sivanandhan uses a booster seat to reach the chessboard.
She's Britain's youngest women's chess champion and the youngest person overall to represent
England internationally in any sport.
On Sunday at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan, she clinched the highest title a female player
can attain, and she'll hold it for life.
She told reporters there, "I want to keep going and keep making history as well instead
of just stop here."
In addition to traveling the world to play chess tournaments, Bodana is in the British
equivalent of sixth grade and is on her way home now to catch up on school assignments.
Lauren Fryer, NPR News, London.
An American company building the new U.S. consulate in Milan has agreed to pay millions
to compensate foreign workers who earned less than $2 an hour.
The nearly $35 million settlement was signed by Alabama-based Caddell Construction.
Nearly 300 workers identified so far will receive on average $56,000, with some receiving
up to $102,000 in unpaid wages and damages.
This is NPR News.
This week on NPR's Newsmakers, Tucker Carlson has broken with President Trump over the war
with Iran and says he warned the president to his face that the war would be a mistake.
And he looked at me and said, "Yes, you're right.
But in the end, we all die anyway.
So it doesn't matter."
Tucker Carlson, this week on NPR's Newsmakers, watch or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

topics.text: President Trump announces construction of steel mill in Iowa expected to create 2,000 jobs by 2030
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito recuses himself from climate change case involving Boulder suing energy companies
SpaceX Starship rocket reaches orbit for first time, deploys Starlink satellites before splashing down in Pacific
Trump administration revokes visas of 27 Latin American officials over corruption accusations including Bolivia's attorney general
Cleveland Orchestra's strike ends after months of bargaining
Bodana Sivanandhan becomes Britain's youngest women's chess champion at Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan
Caddell Construction agrees to pay $35 million settlement to foreign workers for unpaid wages in Milan consulate project
